title: The measure of bliss — a hundred times, a hundred times (2.8)
hook: the Taittiriya tries to put a number on joy, multiplying by a hundred, rung after rung, and then turns the whole ladder upside down
tomorrow: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman

segments.voice: Yesterday: words and mind turn back from it. Your line was beyond words. Did something move you that you didn't try to explain? Today the same chapter does the opposite. It tries to measure. Day three hundred ninety-five.

On a scale of one to ten, how happy are you right now? Doctors ask you to rate pain this way. Apps ask you to rate your mood. We like a number. It feels like proof. Now imagine an ancient teacher sitting with students and trying the same thing on joy itself. Not your joy today. The biggest joy there is. How would you even start? The Taittiriya Upanishad starts with the best life a human being could have. It gives that one number, one unit. And then it starts multiplying.
screen: `RATE IT, ONE TO TEN.` → `A NUMBER FEELS LIKE PROOF.` → `NOW MEASURE JOY ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Section eight is called, in later tradition, the inquiry into bliss. Here's the opening unit. Picture a young man, good, well-read, quick, steady and strong, and suppose the whole earth, full of its wealth, belonged to him. That is one measure of human bliss. Now multiply it by a hundred. That's one bliss of the gandharvas, the heavenly musicians who were once human. A hundred of those, and you reach the divine gandharvas. A hundred of those, the ancestors in their long-lasting world. Then the gods born in heaven. Then the gods who rose there by their deeds. Then the gods. Then Indra, their king. Then Brihaspati, the gods' teacher. Then Prajapati, the lord of creatures. And a hundred of his, the bliss of Brahman. The numbers get absurd fast, which is the point. But here's the line the whole passage turns on. At every single rung, the text adds: and so too for the one who knows the Veda and is not struck by desire. Shrotriya, akamahata. The learned one, untouched by wanting. So the person who wants nothing already has the bliss of the musicians, the gods, Indra, Prajapati. The ladder is real, and you don't have to climb it. The arithmetic of joy, in this text, isn't addition. It's subtraction. Each want you set down removes what was standing between you and the top. And the very next section brings back yesterday's verse: the one who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing.
screen: `ONE UNIT: THE BEST HUMAN LIFE.` · `TIMES A HUNDRED, RUNG AFTER RUNG.` · `AT EVERY RUNG: THE ONE WITHOUT DESIRE.` · `JOY BY SUBTRACTION.` · then, large: `AKAMAHATA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of subtraction. Sit, and let yourself notice one small want that's present right now. A snack. A message you're waiting for. Wanting this to be over. Don't scold it. Just name it, softly, and set it down for the length of one breath. Then see if there's another, and set that one down too. Between the wants, there may be a moment that needs nothing added. That moment is what the text was measuring. The bell holds the time.
The measure of bliss. Taittiriya 2.8: human joy multiplied by a hundred, rung after rung, up to Brahman, and the same bliss, at every rung, for the one untouched by desire.
Your line: the arithmetic of joy. Today, when you catch yourself thinking I'll be happy when, try subtracting the want instead of adding the thing. Day three hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Vedanta teachers often read the ananda-mimamsa of Taittiriya 2.8 aloud and explain it as a lesson that joy grows as desire falls away, not as possessions grow.

fork.setup: you could own the whole earth and every treasure in it. the Taittiriya says someone else already has a hundred times that joy and more. who?
options: the learned one untouched by desire.
fork.reveal: at every rung, the text says the same bliss belongs to the shrotriya, akamahata: the one who knows the Veda and is not struck by desire.

original.note: Sanskrit ānanda-mīmāṃsā, the inquiry into bliss: the traditional name for Taittiriya 2.8.

trapdoor: what you thought: the more you have, the happier you are.
what it means: the Taittiriya multiplies human bliss by a hundred, rung after rung, then gives every rung to the one without desire.
what a scholar hears: shrotriyasya cākāmahatasya, 'and of the Veda-learned one not struck by desire', repeated at each step of the ladder in 2.8.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.9 (the one who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing)

notes: Rungs given from memory: human; human gandharvas; divine gandharvas; the pitrs whose world lasts long; ajanaja devas; karma devas; devas; Indra; Brihaspati; Prajapati; Brahman. Please check order and the gloss 'gandharvas who were once human' for manushya-gandharvas.
2.8 also opens with 'from fear of it the wind blows, the sun rises', not used here.
'Joy by subtraction' is the script's summary of the akamahata refrain, not a textual phrase.
The name ananda-mimamsa for this section is traditional; confirm.
